A lot of my work is with school librarians, and I've been noticing a big shift in the kinds of questions they're asking. Back in the day, I'd get asked, "I need to update my collection of books. What should I get?" Now that's an old way of thinking, and there are much better ways to consider what to add to a school library.
As a member of the Association of Young Adult Librarians and Library Advocates (AYALA), I recently participated in a panel discussion, and I wanted to share what I shared with the participants.
1. Start with What You Already Have
You might be thinking, "There are so many choices, how do I begin?" The first step is to make sure you're keeping track of the books that you do have in your library. I would encourage you to not just keep track of the books, but to make an inventory of your collection.
Why?
When you know what you have and what you don't, it makes it much easier to figure out what you need to get next.
You can't figure out what you need if you don't know what you have.
Once you know what you have, then you can begin to consider what you need.
It also means that you'll be able to have a more informed conversation with your administrator or other decision makers when it comes time to ask for more money.
How to do it:
1. Check your inventory.
If you're in a digital library environment, there are several ways to do this. If you are, or if you're in a library that has a computer that is logged into the online library catalog, you can look at your reports. If you're not, you can ask someone else who is to pull the report for you. If you don't have an online catalog, then you can write down a list of all the books you have in the library.
2. Go through each book and assign it a grade level (for example, "3-5" or "7-12").
Some software will have this pre-assigned for you, but I've found that it's important to really think about what grade level it's best suited for. For example, a "4-6" level book might be just fine for 4th graders, but if you have 6th graders, it might be a little too easy.
3. Now that you know what books you have, think about what you want to add.
The best way to do this is to ask your students what they want to read. If you're not sure how to do this, check out these ideas for ways to ask your students what they want to read.
If you're looking for something to get you started, check out some of my book lists.
2. Consider the Genre
Once you have a good idea of what your library needs, you'll want to make sure that you're getting books from a variety of genres. It's also important to consider the types of books that you have. If you're like me, you probably have a lot of classics. If that's the case, you'll want to make sure that you're adding in some nonfiction and other types of books.
3. Consider the Tone
You'll also want to consider the tone of the books that you're getting. I'm a big fan of the book The Arrival, by Shaun Tan. It's a great book about immigration, but it's also a fantastic read aloud.
It's also a fantastic book to give to teachers, so that they can have a better understanding of what immigrants experience when they come to a new country.
4. Consider the Type of Book
The type of book you're getting will also be very important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting both fiction and nonfiction books. This is especially important if you're teaching a class that is made up of both boys and girls. If you're not, you'll want to make sure that you're getting books for both boys and girls.
5. Consider the Age of the Books
The age of the books is also important. It's easy to get caught up in the newest books that are coming out, but it's important to consider what the age of the books is.
I've found that the older books are the best. They're often written by authors who were in their 20s when they wrote them, and they're more likely to be funny.
6. Consider the Theme
Themes are also important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting books that have a variety of themes. I'm a big fan of the book Wonder, by R.J. Palacio. It's a great book about a boy with a facial deformity, and it has a wonderful theme of acceptance.
7. Consider the Author
The author is also important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting books that have authors who are well-known. This will help you to get books that are going to be more popular.
8. Consider the Title
The title is also important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting books that have titles that are going to be easy for your students to remember. I've found that the books that have simple titles are the best.
9. Consider the Cover
The cover is also important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting books that have covers that are interesting. I've found that the books that have covers that are different from the books that I've seen before are the best.
10. Consider the Price
The price is also important. You'll want to make sure that you're getting books that are going to be affordable. I've found that the books that are priced under $10 are the best.
I hope that you found this information helpful. I'm always looking for ways to improve, so please leave a comment if you have any ideas.

The "Families First Coronavirus Response Act" proposal would provide two weeks of paid sick leave and two months of paid family and medical leave.
In addition, the proposal would offer food stamp benefits to those who are ineligible to receive them. It would also expand access to low-income people to the National School Lunch Program and provide funding for senior meals.
The proposal also expands nutrition benefits for women and their children and would make school lunches available for children during the school closure period.
The proposal would also expand Unemployment Insurance and offer tax credits to small businesses and large corporations.
Sen. Cory Booker, D-New Jersey, is working on the proposal.
The goal is to get it passed this week.

The poll finds that there is significant political division on many issues, including the U.S. economy (46% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents say the U.S. economy is in good shape, compared with just 20% of Democrats and Democratic leaners), climate change (68% of Republicans and Republican leaners say climate change is not a threat, compared with just 31% of Democrats), and healthcare (45% of Republicans and Republican leaners say the healthcare system is working well, compared with 30% of Democrats). There is much more agreement on other issues, including reducing gun violence (68% of both parties support this), lowering college costs (63% of both parties support this), and limiting immigration (64% of both parties support this).
It is unclear how the political polarization of the electorate will influence the upcoming 2020 elections, but it is likely that these political divisions will continue and likely widen.
The poll was conducted Sept. 16-18 among a nationally representative sample of 1,005 adults. The margin of sampling error for the full sample is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

There is a common misconception that when someone dies, their property and possessions will automatically go to their nearest surviving relative.
But that’s not always the case.
Here’s what happens when a person dies without a will in Illinois, how you can make sure your estate goes where you want it to, and what to do when someone dies and leaves no will.
Why It’s Important to Have a Will
If you die without a will, your spouse or children may not inherit everything that they’re legally entitled to.
Your property could be divided unevenly and given to people you didn’t choose. This can cause financial and emotional distress to your surviving family members.
Even if you have no assets, your family will still have to deal with your death, but they won’t have a say in where your possessions end up.
Having a will in place means that you can specify who you want to inherit your estate, avoiding conflicts or disagreements that can make things worse.
If you’re married and don’t have children, your spouse will still have rights to inherit your assets.
Without a will, their rights might be different to those who are not married to you. In some situations, spouses may be entitled to your entire estate.
In other situations, they may only inherit part of your estate or receive nothing.
Without a will, your surviving spouse may not have the same rights as someone who is not married to you.
If you die without a will, your assets will likely go to your spouse or children, as long as they survive you and are legally entitled to inherit.
But, without a will, the laws of intestacy will determine what happens to your assets and whether your spouse or children are entitled to your estate.

I am writing to you at 2:38 am, two days past the due date for the fifth edition of The Gradient and just before I take off from Denver for what should be a quick trip to Kansas City. The flight from Denver to Kansas City is a short, three-hour, one-stop flight via Oklahoma City and it is one of the least expensive flights I’ve ever been on, so I hope to make it through my writing/editing project and the rest of my evening.
What should happen today is that I should be at my desk, working on The Gradient and I should be at home this evening, not in the backseat of a car with some of the most incredibly kind-hearted people I know, watching them try to figure out the best way to support me and keep me as safe as possible from a bad storm. There’s been a lot of drama building up since we met in November to plan this event and I don’t think any of us thought it would still be going on weeks later. The last time I saw my friend, she asked me to speak at her memorial and I hope to make it.
If you’re reading this, you’ve likely known about what’s going on since January. If you haven’t heard from me in the past couple of weeks, this is why.
When you think about it, the storm has a lot in common with the loss of a loved one. It changes your life. It makes your world spin more slowly and with less certainty. It requires all your energy and attention, even though you’re not supposed to give it all to it. And it makes you anxious and afraid, even if it’s not actually about the storm.
